summary: The IMAP UIDBATCHES extension lets clients get UID ranges that split a mailbox into equally sized batches. Clients can then run FETCH, SEARCH, and STORE on batches, controlling resource use and response sizes, which helps especially with UIDONLY mode.

plainLanguage.summary: A huge mailbox is split into equal piles so a program can handle one pile at a time.

questions: how does uidbatches split a mailbox
what is the minimum batch size in uidbatches
subtitle: An IMAP command that hands a client ready-made UID ranges for working through a big mailbox in equal batches.

tldr.problem: Clients often want to process a large mailbox in fixed-size batches, but sequence-number tricks are costly for servers and are not available at all in UIDONLY mode.
tldr.mechanism: A new UIDBATCHES command takes a batch size and optionally a batch range, and the server replies with UID ranges, highest UIDs first, that split the mailbox into batches of up to that size.
tldr.outcome: Clients can run FETCH, SEARCH and STORE on one batch at a time. To protect servers, batch sizes have a 500 minimum and clients may only re-run the command in limited circumstances.

today: RFC 10022 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why UIDBATCHES Exists
sections.content:
The UIDBATCHES extension lets an IMAP client get UID ranges that split a mailbox's messages into evenly sized batches. It works with both IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501) and IMAP4rev2 (RFC 9051).

The main goal is to let a client decide in advance how many messages each command touches. This is most useful with UIDONLY mode (RFC 9586), where the client has no sequence numbers and so cannot easily build batches the usual way.

The RFC also explains the idea as shorthand for a UID SEARCH that lists sequence numbers at multiples of the batch size, but with a special code path that servers can optimize. The PARTIAL extension (RFC 9394) pages through results instead, whereas UIDBATCHES fixes the batches up front.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have a giant pile of letters, it is easier to cut it into equal stacks first. This extension asks the server to do the cutting.

sections.title: The UIDBATCHES Command
sections.content:
A server advertises support with the UIDBATCHES capability. The command takes a message count per batch and an optional batch range, and the server answers with an untagged UIDBATCHES response that MUST include the command tag. The result is OK, NO or BAD.

The server returns ranges in descending UID order. Batch 1 holds the highest UIDs, meaning the most recent messages, batch 2 the next set, and so on. The RFC's example selects a mailbox with 6823 messages, asks for batches of 2000, and gets four ranges: 215295:99696, 99695:20351, 20350:7830 and 7829:1. Each holds up to 2,000 messages, except the last, which has the remaining 823.

New messages cannot appear inside these ranges, so a range's count only goes down as messages are deleted. A client should put newly arrived messages into a new batch starting after the highest returned UID.
sections.plainLanguage: You say how many letters go in each stack, and the clerk tells you where each stack starts and ends. The newest letters are in stack one.

sections.title: Batch Ranges, Empty Replies and Re-Running
sections.content:
A client may add a batch range such as 10:20 to ask only for those batches. The range MUST be written lowest to highest, and a reversed range like 4:1 is rejected with BAD [CLIENTBUG]. Asking for batches that do not exist returns only those that exist, or an empty UIDBATCHES response, which the server MUST still send. Clients MUST NOT request a range spanning more than 100,000 messages, and the server MAY reject such a request with NO [TOOMANY].

Computing batches can be expensive, so the client may resend UIDBATCHES only if a different mailbox was selected, more than N/2 messages were expunged, or more than N/2 new messages arrived, where N is the batch size. Otherwise the client MUST NOT resend it. The server SHOULD reject abusive repeats with NO and the LIMIT response code.

For mailboxes above 100,000 messages, the server MAY reply NO [TOOMANY] to a request for all batches, so the client may choose to always use batch ranges. The server MUST at least support returning ranges spanning 100,000 messages.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for just some stacks. You also should not keep asking the clerk to redo the stacks unless the pile has really changed a lot.

sections.title: Batch Size Rules
sections.content:
Clients MUST request at least 500 messages per batch, and the server MUST support batch sizes of 500 or larger. A smaller request gets NO [TOOFEW]. The floor exists so clients cannot use the command to rebuild sequence numbers, which would undermine UIDONLY mode.

A server MUST NOT return a range with more messages than requested, and it SHOULD stay within 90% of the requested size. It may return smaller batches when that makes its implementation simpler, or when messages are expunged while the command runs. The RFC gives an example of three batches of a requested 1,000 holding 990, 977 and 1,000 messages, and clients MUST cope with such variation. If the requested size equals or exceeds the mailbox size, the server MUST return one range covering all messages.

Returned UIDs need not exist. A range such as 163886:99703 may start and end at UIDs with no message, so clients MUST NOT assume messages exist there. The last range ends at UID 1 so the client knows it is the last.
sections.plainLanguage: Stacks cannot be tiny, and a stack should never be bigger than you asked for. Stacks may be a little smaller, and the ends of the stacks may be only marks, not real letters.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Extensions
sections.content:
With UIDONLY, clients SHOULD use UIDBATCHES to get UID ranges rather than building batches from sequence numbers, which UIDONLY forbids.

With MESSAGELIMIT (RFC 9738), a client SHOULD request batches no larger than the server's announced per-command message limit, and MAY pick a smaller batch size.

With SEARCHRES (RFC 5182), UIDBATCHES is not a SEARCH command, so a server MUST NOT store its result in the $ variable.
sections.plainLanguage: The new command plays nicely with other rules. It stays within sizes the server allows and it does not mess with the saved search result.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The ABNF defines the command as UIDBATCHES followed by a batch size and an optional batch range. Both are non-zero numbers, and the range is two numbers joined by a colon. The response is UIDBATCHES with a search correlator and an optional comma-separated list of UID ranges. The new response codes are TOOFEW and TOOMANY, and keywords are case-insensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: This part writes the exact spelling of the command so every program reads it the same way.

sections.title: Security and Operational Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says the extension adds no new security issues beyond IMAP4rev1 and IMAP4rev2. The concern it designed against is clients forcing servers into heavy work by asking for batch calculations over and over. The re-run limits and the batch size constraints are meant to mitigate this, and servers are strongly advised to enforce them and SHOULD track UIDBATCHES requests per mailbox, because malicious or buggy clients could otherwise exhaust resources.

Servers may reject violations with LIMIT, TOOFEW or TOOMANY. IANA has added the UIDBATCHES capability and the TOOMANY and TOOFEW response codes to its registries. Because this is new code on both sides, the RFC calls for rigorous testing.
sections.plainLanguage: The server should not let anyone keep asking for the same sorting again and again, because that wastes its effort.

data.title: UIDBATCHES with batch size 2000
data.code:
C: A142 SELECT INBOX
S: * 6823 EXISTS
S: * OK [UIDNEXT 215296] Predicted next UID
C: A143 UIDBATCHES 2000
S: * UIDBATCHES (TAG "A143") 215295:99696,99695:20351,20350:7830,7829:1
S: A143 OK UIDBATCHES Completed
